summary: This document specifies a method to split control plane and user plane in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network. Existing options let a mobile access gateway separate them, but no way existed to signal such a split to the local mobility anchor.

eli5.summary: In a mobile network, one box can handle both instructions and data. This RFC lets them be handled by different machines.

questions: pmipv6 control plane user plane separation
split cp up proxy mobile ipv6
what is the lma user-plane address option
how to separate control plane and user plane in proxy mobile ipv6
subtitle: A new Proxy Mobile IPv6 option lets the anchor use one address for signaling and another for user traffic.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile access gateway split its control and user planes, but gives the local mobility anchor no way to do the same, so signaling and user traffic must share one LMA address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the LMA User-Plane Address mobility option, carried in Proxy Binding Update and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement messages, which tells the MAG which LMA address to use for the user-plane tunnel.
tldr.outcome: An LMA can now use a different IP address for user-plane traffic than for control-plane traffic, so the two functions can scale or sit in separate places.

today: RFC 7389 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2014. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why Split the Control and User Plane
sections.content:
A Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) network has two main entities: the local mobility anchor (LMA) and the mobile access gateway (MAG). Between them runs a control plane, which carries signaling such as the Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) that set up a mobility binding, and a user plane, which carries the mobile node's IP traffic through a bidirectional tunnel.

The RFC says widely deployed mobility systems for wireless communications need separate IP transport for user-plane and control-plane traffic. It gives examples. In a WLAN, the MAG control plane could sit on the Access Controller while the user plane sits on the access points. An LMA's two planes may also need different scaling, or the control plane may be centralized in one place while the user plane is spread across several.

The problem is that PMIPv6 requires the LMA to tie the tunnel source address to the target address of control messages from the MAG. The LMA therefore could not use a separate address for user traffic.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the part that makes the plans and the part that carries the traffic should live in different places. Before this RFC, the anchor could only have one address for both jobs.

sections.title: Terminology and Existing MAG-Side Support
sections.content:
The RFC introduces four address names. The LMA Control-Plane Address (LMA-CPA) is used for control traffic with the MAG, and the LMA User-Plane Address (LMA-UPA) is used for user-plane traffic. The MAG has matching MAG-CPA and MAG-UPA addresses; the MAG-UPA is also called the Alternate Care-of Address.

The MAG side was already covered. RFC 6463 defines the Alternate IPv4 Care-of Address option and RFC 6275 defines an Alternate Care-of Address option for IPv6. A MAG can offer one in its PBU, and if the LMA supports it, the tunnel runs between the LMA address and the MAG's alternate address. No matching option let the LMA offer an alternate tunnel endpoint to the MAG.

For bookkeeping, the Binding Update List entry kept by the LMA and MAG gains two fields: the LMA address that carries user-plane traffic and the LMA address that handles control-plane traffic.
sections.eli5: The gateway already had a way to say 'send packages to my other door'. The anchor had no way to say the same thing back, and this RFC fixes that.

sections.title: The LMA User-Plane Address Option
sections.content:
The new LMA User-Plane Address mobility option is used in PBU and PBA messages. A message can carry zero, one or two instances. If there are two, one must be for IPv4 transport and the other for IPv6 transport. The option has an alignment requirement of 8n+2.

Its fields are Type (59), Length (the option length in octets, excluding the Type and Length fields), a Reserved field that the sender MUST set to zero and the receiver MUST ignore, and the LMA User-Plane Address itself, which is a 32-bit IPv4 or 128-bit IPv6 address.

In a PBU, the MAG uses the option only to signal support: the address field MUST be either zero-length or all zeros (4 octets for IPv4, 16 octets for IPv6). In a PBA, the LMA MUST put its real IPv4 or IPv6 user-plane address in the field. The choice of encapsulation for the user plane follows RFC 5213 and RFC 5844.
sections.eli5: The MAG sends a blank note saying 'I understand this'. The anchor answers with a note that has the real address of its package door.

sections.title: Deciding Whether the Feature Is Used
sections.content:
The RFC defines a configuration variable, Domain-wide-LMA-UPA-Support, which must be configurable on every LMA and MAG, must survive reboots and restarts, and must be the same for every LMA and MAG in the PMIPv6 domain. Its default is zero on both sides.

With the variable at zero on the MAG, the MAG MUST include the option in its PBU to show it supports the feature; if the option is absent, the LMA SHALL disable the feature for that session. With the variable at zero on the LMA, the LMA MUST NOT include the option in the PBA unless the MAG sent it in the PBU.

Setting the variable to one means the whole domain supports the feature. The MAG MAY then leave the option out of its PBU, and the LMA SHOULD include the option in the PBA even if the PBU lacked it.
sections.eli5: By default the two sides check with each other first. If everyone in the network already agrees, they can skip the check.

sections.title: Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The control-plane and user-plane parts of a MAG or LMA are usually in one physical entity, and then the link between them is internal. They can be put on separate IP nodes, but the protocol between those nodes is outside this RFC. The text lists OpenFlow, ForCES, use of routing infrastructure and vendor-specific approaches as possible options without mandating any.

When the LMA planes are on separate nodes, the node hosting the LMA user plane must meet the address anchoring requirement from RFC 5213 and RFC 5844. It must be a topological anchor point for the IP address or prefixes allocated to the mobile node.

The user-plane tunnel may use GRE, IP-in-IP or UDP encapsulation, as in the RFC's Figure 1.
sections.eli5: If the two jobs are done by two different machines, those machines need a way to talk. This RFC does not say how, but the package machine must still be the place where the mobile device's address lives.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
PMIPv6 signaling between MAG and LMA must be protected with end-to-end security associations giving integrity and data origin authentication, and IPsec is mandatory to implement. Nodes hosting the control-plane functions must still meet this. For the user plane, the nodes must support IPsec but using it to protect user traffic stays optional, as before.

The LMA-UPA in the option MUST be a valid address under the administrative control of the LMA functional block. If the LMA control and user planes are on different entities, control messages between them that carry the option MUST be protected with integrity and data origin authentication.

IANA allocated Type value 59 for the new option in the Mobility Options registry.
sections.eli5: The messages still need a lock and a signature, and the anchor may only hand out addresses it really controls.
